# Unequal-radius conditional surface densities and projectively weighted parity repair

Status: proved auxiliary upgrade, subject to the already audited ordinary
surface-disintegration and conditional-ball theorem dependencies below.
No OC conclusion is asserted.

The new input is to use different shrinking radii at the two endpoint
faces. It improves the density exponent from `d-1` to `d-1-m`, where
`m` is the common face dimension. A same-body argument also gives a
continuous concave-power representative of every positive conditional
density. With the positive part of a common concave factor `H` and a
common positive convex denominator `L` (in particular an affine one),
the weight `g H_+/L^d` satisfies
exactly the negative-power envelope required by midpoint density repair.

## 1. Dependencies and notation

We use the proved, independently audited statements in

* `candidate d7f1891e34b3ec5a`;
* `candidate f38040720425d155`;
* `candidate 1bc960743a4bce34`;
* `candidate 93c94ac2c5c85584`;
* `candidate 9764a982661d3ddc`;
* `candidate 5ea88513a25f2f4b`.

In particular, if `A,B,K` are full-dimensional convex bodies in `R^d`,
`d>=2`, `(A+B)/2 subset K`, and a normal `n` is a tight support normal,
the relevant nonzero conditional surface laws `mu_-,mu_+,mu_0`, taken
relative to ONE common normal measure, have exposed faces of the same
dimension `m` and the same tangent direction. They are equivalent to
Euclidean `H_m` in the corresponding face interiors.

Outside one fixed exceptional normal set, their conditional ball masses
satisfy, for ALL open ball centers and all positive radii,

```
mu_0(B_((a+b)/2)((x+y)/2))
 >= [(mu_-(B_a(x))^(1/delta)
      +mu_+(B_b(y))^(1/delta))/2]^delta,       delta=d-1,       (1)
```

whenever both endpoint ball masses are positive. The same theorem can
be applied to the self-triple `(K,K,K)`. Its degree-one homogeneity
allows every finite collection of such statements to use the same
enlarged normal reference. No densities from different normal references
are multiplied or compared without this adjustment.

For `r>0`, write

```
P_r(a,b)=[(a^(1/r)+b^(1/r))/2]^r.
```

For `m>0`, write

```
N_m(a,b)=[(a^(-1/m)+b^(-1/m))/2]^(-m)
```

when `a,b>0`, with value zero if either input is zero.

## 2. Unequal radii give the intrinsic exponent

Assume first `m>0`. Let `E_-`, `E_+` be the full-measure endpoint
differentiation sets supplied by the conditional-ball theorem, with
finite positive density values `g_-(x)`, `g_+(y)`. Use its upper-density
representative `g_0^+` at every possible middle point.

Fix ANY pair `x in E_-`, `y in E_+`. Apply (1) with endpoint radii
`epsilon a`, `epsilon b`, where `a,b>0` are arbitrary fixed numbers.
Divide by `omega_m epsilon^m` and let `epsilon` decrease to zero.
Endpoint differentiation and degree-one homogeneity give

```
g_0^+((x+y)/2) ((a+b)/2)^m
 >= [(g_-(x)^(1/delta) a^(m/delta)
      +g_+(y)^(1/delta) b^(m/delta))/2]^delta.              (2)
```

The left side is the relevant upper limit, so the assertion does not
presume differentiation at the middle point. It holds for every
`a,b>0` for this fixed endpoint pair, because (1) held for every ball
pair on the same exceptional-set complement.

If `0<m<delta`, put `r=delta-m>0` and normalize `a+b=2`. The function

```
A a^(m/delta)+B b^(m/delta),
A=g_-(x)^(1/delta), B=g_+(y)^(1/delta),
```

is strictly concave on this line segment. Its unique positive maximum
occurs at

```
a:b = g_-(x)^(1/r):g_+(y)^(1/r).
```

Substitution into (2) gives the exact stronger bound

```
g_0^+((x+y)/2) >= P_r(g_-(x),g_+(y)),
r=d-1-m.                                                   (3)
```

For completeness, writing `U=g_-^(1/r)`, `V=g_+^(1/r)`, the maximizing
radii are `a=2U/(U+V)`, `b=2V/(U+V)`. The expression before the
`delta` power in (2) then equals
`2^(-r/delta)(U+V)^(r/delta)`, whose `delta` power is `P_r(g_-,g_+)`.

If `m=delta`, the right side before its `delta` power is affine in
`a,b`. Letting `a` tend to two and `b` to zero, and then reversing the
roles, gives

```
g_0^+((x+y)/2) >= max(g_-(x),g_+(y)).                        (4)
```

All radii used in (1) remain strictly positive; the limit in their ratio
is taken only after (2) has been obtained.

If `m=0`, each conditional face is a single point. Balls of sufficiently
small positive radius contain its entire conditional atom. Hence (1)
gives directly

```
g_0 >= P_delta(g_-,g_+).                                    (5)
```

This agrees with (3) with `r=delta`. Here `g_i` denotes the positive
atom mass, with respect to `H_0` on the one-point face.

## 3. Continuous representatives and actual concavity on every face

The preceding bounds require only upper target densities. We now prove
that actual conditional surface laws have stronger regularity, and do
so without citing an almost-everywhere functional-equation theorem.

Let `mu` be a nonzero conditional surface law of a body at one of the
normals where its self-triple ball inequalities hold. Let `F` be the
exposed face, let `m=dim F>0`, and put `O=relint F`. Identify its affine
hull isometrically with `R^m`.

Define, for `epsilon>0`,

```
f_epsilon(x)=mu(B_epsilon(x))/(omega_m epsilon^m),
h_epsilon(x)=f_epsilon(x)^(1/delta),     x in O.             (6)
```

Each `f_epsilon` is continuous: it is the convolution of the integrable
conditional density with a normalized ball indicator, and translation
is continuous in `L^1`. It is positive on `O`, since the support of
`mu` is the whole face. The self-triple form of (1), with equal radii,
gives midpoint concavity of `h_epsilon` on `O`. Continuity upgrades
midpoint concavity to full concavity, first for dyadic weights and then
for every weight by taking limits.

There are uniform local upper bounds for these concave functions. Fix
`x in O` and choose `r>0` with `B_(2r)(x) subset O`. For every
`y in B_r(x)`, concavity and nonnegativity give

```
h_epsilon(y)
 >= (h_epsilon(x)+h_epsilon(2y-x))/2
 >= h_epsilon(x)/2.
```

Also Fubini in the affine face space gives

```
integral_(R^m) f_epsilon = mu(F).
```

Consequently

```
omega_m r^m (h_epsilon(x)/2)^delta <= mu(F).                (7)
```

Choosing `r` uniformly on compact subsets proves uniform local bounds.
Nonnegative concave functions that are uniformly bounded on a slightly
larger compact neighborhood have a uniform Lipschitz bound on the
smaller neighborhood: restrict to any line, extend a fixed positive
distance in both directions, and bound its intermediate secant slopes
by the two longer secants and the common value bounds. Thus this
family is locally equicontinuous.

Arzela--Ascoli and a compact exhaustion of `O` give locally uniform
convergence along every subsequence after a further subsequence. The
limit is a finite nonnegative continuous concave function `h`.
Lebesgue differentiation gives

```
f_epsilon(x) -> g(x)  for H_m-almost every x,
```

where `g` is the original conditional density. Hence every subsequential
limit is `g^(1/delta)` almost everywhere. Two continuous functions on
`O` equal almost everywhere are equal everywhere, so the limit is
unique and the whole family converges locally uniformly to `h`.

Define the continuous density representative `g_c=h^delta`. It is
positive throughout `O`. Indeed a nonnegative concave function that
vanishes at an interior point must vanish everywhere: express that
point as a strict convex combination of any other point and a nearby
point in the opposite direction. This would contradict positivity of
the original density almost everywhere.

Since `mu=g_c H_m` and `g_c` is continuous in `O`, every point of `O`
is now a differentiation point, with density `g_c(x)`. In particular its
upper-density representative also equals `g_c` at every such point.

Apply (3)--(4) to the self-triple using these representatives. We obtain:

* if `0<m<delta`, then `g_c^(1/(delta-m))` is a positive concave
  function on `O`;
* if `m=delta`, then `g_c` is constant on `O`.

For the second assertion, (4) says
`g_c((x+y)/2)>=max(g_c(x),g_c(y))`. At two sufficiently close interior
points `x,y`, both reflected points `2x-y` and `2y-x` remain inside
`O`; applying this inequality gives both `g_c(x)>=g_c(y)` and the
reverse. Thus `g_c` is locally constant and, by connectedness, constant
on `O`.

These are intrinsic density statements. They do not assert smoothness
or rectifiability of the set of normal labels. Constants may depend
without bound on the normal.

## 4. Every relative-interior endpoint pair has a finite target value

For a triple as in Section 1, include the three self-triples in the
finite common exceptional-set choice. Select the continuous positive
representative from Section 3 on each positive-dimensional face
interior, or the atom mass for a zero-dimensional face.

For ANY `x in relint A(n)` and `y in relint B(n)`, their midpoint
lies in the relative interior of `K(n)`. Indeed the endpoint tangent
spaces coincide and have dimension `m`. A small relative ball about
`x` lies in `A(n)`, and a small relative ball about `y` lies in
`B(n)`; their midpoint contains a relative ball about `(x+y)/2`.
This midpoint ball lies in `K(n)` and its affine hull is the full
affine hull of that face.

Thus (3)--(5) hold with the continuous target representative `g_0`,
for EVERY pair in the two face interiors. Those are marginal-full
sets, and all target values used here are finite. This strengthens,
and does not invalidate, the upper-density version of Section 2.

## 5. A common concave numerator factor and convex denominator

Let `w_-,w_+,w_0` be the physical endpoint and midpoint points, including
any finite base coordinates. Suppose `H_i>=0`, `L_i>0` satisfy

```
H_0 >= (H_-+H_+)/2,
L_0 <= (L_-+L_+)/2.                                       (8)
```

This is assured by a COMMON concave function `H` and a COMMON convex
function `L` on the physical convex domain. Different contact-dependent
functions assigned after seeing a label do not satisfy (8) automatically
and are not covered.

Assume `H_-,H_+>0`, as is necessary for positive weighted source density,
and define

```
F_i = g_i H_i / L_i^d.                                    (9)
```

We claim that the exact repair envelopes are

```
F_0 >= N_m(F_-,F_+)            if m>0,
F_0 >= min(F_-,F_+)            if m=0.                     (10)
```

Write `r=d-1-m` and `s=r+1=d-m`. If `r>0`, inequality (3) says that
`U_0>= (U_-+U_+)/2`, where `U_i=g_i^(1/r)`. The function

```
(U,H) -> (U^r H)^(1/(r+1))
```

is nondecreasing in both variables and concave on the nonnegative
quadrant. A direct proof of concavity is the identity

```
(U^r H)^(1/(r+1))
 = inf_(a>0) [r a U + a^(-r) H]/(r+1),                    (11)
```

verified by differentiation when both inputs are positive and by
limits at zero. An infimum of affine functions is concave. Therefore

```
R_i=(g_i H_i)^(1/s)
```

satisfies

```
R_0 >= (R_-+R_+)/2.                                      (12)
```

If `r=0`, inequality (4) gives `g_0>=max(g_-,g_+)` and `s=1`.
Then (8) directly implies

```
R_0=g_0 H_0
 >= (g_- H_-+g_+ H_+)/2,
```

so (12) still holds.

When `m>0`, put `p=d/m>1`. A rearrangement of (9) is

```
F_i^(-1/m)=L_i^p/R_i^(p-1).                              (13)
```

The function `Q(L,R)=L^p/R^(p-1)=R(L/R)^p` is convex for
`L,R>0`: it is the perspective of the convex function `t^p`.
This follows directly from Jensen, since for positive `R_1,R_2`
the ratio of their weighted numerator sum to their weighted
denominator sum is a convex combination of the two ratios, with
weights proportional to the denominators. Moreover `Q` is increasing
in its first variable and decreasing in its second variable, because
`partial_L Q=p L^(p-1) R^(-(p-1))>0` and
`partial_R Q=-(p-1)L^p R^(-p)<0`.
Using (8), (12), and then convexity gives

```
F_0^(-1/m)
 <= Q((L_-+L_+)/2,(R_-+R_+)/2)
 <= [F_-^(-1/m)+F_+^(-1/m)]/2.
```

This is precisely the first inequality in (10).

If `m=0`, then `s=d`, and `F_i=(R_i/L_i)^d`. Equation (12) and
the convex inequality for `L` imply

```
R_0/L_0 >= (R_-+R_+)/(L_-+L_+)
          >= min(R_-/L_-,R_+/L_+),
```

which proves the second inequality in (10).

If either endpoint weighted density vanishes, the needed capacity
inequality has right side zero, so the same conclusion follows without
using negative powers at zero.

On the relative interior of one fixed face, these calculations give a
literal convexity statement, not just an almost-everywhere envelope:
where `H>0`, the function

```
(g H/L^d)^(-1/m)
```

is convex for `m>0`. Indeed Section 3 gives concavity of the required
power of `g`, (11) gives concavity of `R`, and the preceding decreasing
perspective argument proves convexity. For `m=0` the face is a point.

There is a useful signed-numerator extension. A COMMON concave function
`H` need not be nonnegative everywhere: one may use `H_+=max(H,0)`
in (9). If both endpoint weighted densities are positive, both endpoint
values of `H` are positive; concavity then makes its middle value
positive and gives (8) for these three positive parts. If one endpoint
weighted density is zero, the needed right side of (10) is zero.
Thus the envelope remains valid. No false global concavity assertion
about `H_+` is used. The domain `{H>0}` on each face is convex, so the
literal inverse-power convexity statement holds on that domain.

The direction of curvature of the denominator is essential: a positive
maximum of affine denominators is permitted by its convexity. Their
minimum is generally concave and does not satisfy (8). Contact-cell
arguments for such a minimum need an additional equality and are not
included in this theorem.

## 6. Ordinary weighted midpoint repair

Fix one tight normal and the corresponding common face dimension `m`.
Suppose the finite conditional endpoint measures `gamma_-,gamma_+`
have equal mass and satisfy

```
gamma_i <= F_i H_m
```

on their respective faces. Let an arbitrary old coupling have midpoint
law `rho_old`. Suppose also the weighted target measure `F_0 H_m` is
finite. Then there exists another coupling of exactly the same endpoint
marginals with midpoint law `rho` such that

```
rho_old <=cx rho,       rho <= F_0 H_m.                     (14)
```

For `m>0`, this is the variable-density barycentric selection theorem
with the envelope (10). The source good sets are the two relative face
interiors on which the weighted density is positive. They carry all
source mass. The optimizer's inverse endpoint maps first prove absolute
continuity of its output; the weighted area formula and the common
positive-semidefinite derivative identity then give
`h<=N_m(F_-(X_-),F_+(X_+))<=F_0` almost everywhere. The fixed finite
target measure supplies the weakly closed capacity class, and the
compact finite-intersection argument gives convex-order domination of
the prescribed old law. No uniform bound on the conditional densities
is needed. For `m=0`, the corresponding discrete inverse-endpoint
argument uses the minimum bound in (10).

This uses the actual weight `gH/L^d`. It does not manufacture an
unweighted higher-dimensional convex body having that density.

## 7. Weighted normal-preserving parity repair

Here is the precise global variant. Use the setting and definitions of
`candidate 9764a982661d3ddc`:

* `P` is finite and lattice-complete in its convex hull;
* `K_z` are positive full-dimensional compatible fibers in `R^d`;
* `C` is their canonical convex hull with exact sampled fibers;
* `eta` is the sum of their physical normal-bundle surface measures.

For each normal `n`, let `H(n,w)` be concave in the full physical
coordinate `w=(z,x)` on `C`, and let `L(n,w)` be convex there. Assume

```
L>0,
W(n,w)=H(n,w)_+/L(n,w)^d
```

is Borel and bounded on the compact physical normal-bundle range and
on the finitely many auxiliary pair-average ranges. For example it
suffices that `H,L` are continuous in `(n,w)` and `L` is bounded below
by a positive constant. Define the finite weighted surface measure

```
omega = W eta.                                             (15)
```

Let `gamma_-,gamma_+<=omega` be equal-mass endpoint measures. Suppose
an old coupling has a common normal label at both endpoints, integer
midpoints, and its midpoints lie on the actual target support graph.
Then there is a replacement with those same endpoint marginals, still
normal-preserving, whose new midpoint law satisfies

```
rho <= 2^n omega,                                          (16)
```

and whose conditional midpoint law dominates the old law in convex
order within each normal and each endpoint parity class. The same
marked-source martingale preservation as in the unweighted theorem
holds. Thus a source mark's joint distribution with normal and parity,
and its conditional midpoint mean, may be retained.

Here are the modifications required in the full proof, so (16) is not
an assertion that arbitrary reweighting preserves the old theorem.

1. Include every actual fiber body and every pair-average body
   `M_zw=(K_z+K_w)/2` in the common UNWEIGHTED normal reference `sigma`.
   Include all their self-triples as well as all cross-pair and actual
   tight-target triples in the finite exceptional-set choice. The
   homogeneous change of reference preserves (1)--(5).

2. At a fixed good normal, all positive conditional original faces and
   relevant pair-average faces have the common dimension and tangent
   space established in the unweighted theorem. Their weighted
   conditional capacities are exactly `g_z H_+/L^d` and
   `g_zw H_+/L^d`, with the physical base of a pair-average body equal
   to `(z+w)/2`. Formula (10) applies to every positive endpoint
   tuple. Weighted source mass ignores points where `H<=0`, and the
   positive-endpoint argument at the end of Section 5 applies.

3. Within a single parity class use the same augmented bases consisting
   of the integer base and perpendicular affine face offset. At an
   off-roof output level use the finite sum of the weighted
   pair-average conditional capacities producing that level. At an
   on-roof output level use the actual weighted target conditional
   capacity. The pairwise estimates (10) justify both choices. Their
   finiteness follows from boundedness of `W` and finiteness of the
   original and auxiliary conditional surface laws. Repeated pairs
   do not duplicate the auxiliary reference, which is counting
   measure on distinct augmented levels times `H_m` in the common
   tangent space.

4. Apply mixed variable-density selection to these ceilings. The
   unchanged finite concave support roof provides the global convex
   test `Phi(z,x)=n dot x-h_tilde(z)`. It is nonpositive on every
   possible midpoint and zero on the old midpoint law. Convex-order
   improvement forces its integral, and therefore its value almost
   everywhere on the new law, to remain zero. The new law is on the
   actual support graph. At each physical output base the target
   face's perpendicular affine offset is unique, so there is no
   multiplicity of on-roof capacities. Each parity class therefore
   contributes at most the actual weighted conditional target law.

5. Sum the at most `2^n` classes. For measurable assembly describe the
   final feasible classes in the original compact physical coordinates
   by their fixed conditional marginals, convex-order constraints, and
   domination by the Borel kernel `W mu_z`. Boundedness of `W` gives
   a common finite mass bound. The audited selector applies without
   any measurable choice of tangent frames or continuous density
   representatives. Integrating over `sigma` proves (16).

6. The marked-source reconstruction uses the selected martingale from
   the old midpoint to the new one and then disintegrates the new
   endpoint coupling over its midpoint. It preserves the old mark,
   normal, and parity law, and the tower property preserves its
   conditional midpoint mean. The endpoint pair labels themselves
   need not be preserved, exactly as in the unweighted theorem.

All weights are shared physical functions throughout. In particular
`H` and `L` may depend on the normal, but cannot be chosen separately
for different contact labels within one conditional replacement.

## 8. The one-dimensional surface case

When `d=1`, every positive fiber is an interval and its surface measure
has a unit atom at each of the two outward normals. At a fixed normal,
all original interval endpoints and all auxiliary pair-average
endpoints have the same unweighted conditional atom mass relative to
the common normal reference. Thus `g_0=g_-=g_+`.

For `W=H_+/L`, concavity of the common `H` and convexity of the common
positive `L` give, whenever both endpoint weights are positive,

```
g_0 H_0/L_0 >= min(g_- H_-/L_-,g_+ H_+/L_+).
```

If an endpoint weight is zero the required minimum bound is automatic.

The discrete version of the same augmented-base argument therefore
proves (16) also for `d=1`, with no undefined zero power and without
invoking the `delta=d-1` ball formula. No `d=0` surface assertion is
made.

## 9. Scope of the upgrade

The new theorem proves a precise projectively weighted surface capacity
and supplies genuine concave-power structure on conditional faces. It
does not infer a cap bound from convex order, does not identify a
mixed-integer center, and does not convert arbitrary label-dependent
projective weights into a common physical weight. Those are separate
requirements in any intended use of this theorem for OC.
